# `liber:graphics@1`

Generated reference for the `liber:graphics` package (`graphics.lsidl`). See [the LSIDL language](../../../LSIDL.md).

LiberSystem graphics package - the VALUE TYPES every graphics interface shares.  WHY A PACKAGE OF ITS OWN, WITH NO INTERFACE IN IT. An extent, a rectangle, a pixel format, a colour space and an alpha mode cross the application display interface, the display-device interface and their generated crates. Each interface that declared its own copy would be declaring a DIFFERENT type with the same name: `liber:display@1` had its own `pixel-format` with one member, and a second interface adding a second member would have produced two enumerations that a reader cannot tell apart and a version cannot be declared against.  THESE ARE THE WIRE TYPES AND NOT THE PROGRAM'S TYPES, and the difference is the whole design. What crosses a channel is an unvalidated descriptor somebody else wrote: a pitch that does not cover a row, an extent that overflows when multiplied, a format a reader does not know. The in-process types live in `graphics-core`, are constructed only through checked conversions from these, and every trust boundary crosses in that one direction. Treating the wire record as the program's type would delete the boundary that proves a hostile descriptor was checked, and would tie the in-process layout to a schema this project versions independently.  THE CLOSED SETS BELOW ARE THE PROFILE'S. `Image Colour Profile 1` freezes twelve formats, three alpha modes and eight colour spaces, with a hash over the canonical form; this package carries exactly those, in that order, because a wire enumeration that admitted a thirteenth format would be a format no profile describes and no backend is required to implement.

## Types

### record `extent-2d`

A size in pixels. Zero in either component is a legal EMPTY extent and is not an error: a surface that has not been sized yet, and a damage region that covers nothing, are both ordinary.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `width` | `u32` |  |
| `height` | `u32` |  |

### record `offset-2d`

A position in pixels, from the top-left corner. SIGNED, because a rectangle may be clipped to a surface it starts outside of, and expressing that with an unsigned origin means the clipper has to carry the sign somewhere else.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x` | `i32` |  |
| `y` | `i32` |  |

### record `rect`

A rectangle as an origin and an extent rather than as two corners.  TWO CORNERS ARE TWO WAYS TO SAY ONE THING and one of them is wrong: a rectangle whose second corner is above its first is a rectangle every reader normalises differently, and a normalisation nobody agreed on is a rectangle that differs by a pixel across a boundary. An origin and an extent cannot express it at all.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `origin` | `offset-2d` |  |
| `size` | `extent-2d` |  |

### enum `pixel-format`

The pixel formats `Image Colour Profile 1` freezes, in the profile's own order.  THE NAME STATES THE MEMORY ORDER AND NEVER HOST ENDIANNESS. `B8G8R8A8_UNORM` has blue in its first byte on every machine; a format named for a `u32` value means something different on a big-endian one, which is the ambiguity this naming exists to remove.

### enum `alpha-mode`

What the alpha channel MEANS, which is not something a format says.  A FORMAT WITH AN ALPHA CHANNEL DOES NOT SAY WHETHER THE COLOUR IS MULTIPLIED BY IT. Compositing the two the same way is the classic dark halo, and it is invisible until somebody looks at an edge - so the meaning travels beside the format rather than being inferred from it.

| case | ordinal | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `opaque` | 0 | The alpha channel is present and is not to be read: the image is opaque. |
| `straight` | 1 | Colour is independent of alpha. |
| `premultiplied` | 2 | Colour has already been multiplied by alpha. |

### enum `row-origin`

WHICH ROW IS THE FIRST ONE IN MEMORY.  A scanout is top-down and a captured or firmware-provided buffer can be bottom-up, and an image handed over without saying which is an image that is sometimes upside down. It is not a property of the format and not a property of the device: it is a property of THIS buffer.

| case | ordinal | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `top-left` | 0 |  |
| `bottom-left` | 1 |  |

### record `image-layout`

How the bytes of one image plane are arranged, and what they mean.  `pitch` IS IN BYTES AND MAY EXCEED THE ROW, which is why it is here rather than derived: an aligned allocation, a sub-image of a larger one and a device requirement all produce a pitch larger than `width * bytes-per-pixel`, and a reader that assumed otherwise reads the wrong row. Nothing here is trusted: `graphics-core`'s conversion checks that the pitch covers a row, that the arithmetic does not overflow, and that the buffer holds what the layout claims.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `size` | `extent-2d` |  |
| `pitch` | `u32` |  |
| `format` | `pixel-format` |  |
| `alpha` | `alpha-mode` |  |
| `color-space` | `color-space` |  |
| `origin` | `row-origin` |  |

### record `damage-region`

The rectangles of an image that changed, with an explicit WHOLE-SURFACE answer.  A LIST AND A FLAG RATHER THAN AN EMPTY LIST MEANING EVERYTHING. An empty list is the one case two implementations read in opposite ways - nothing changed, or everything did - and the difference is a frame that is not drawn versus a frame that is drawn entirely. Stating it removes the question: `whole` is the answer to "I do not know what changed", and an empty `rects` with `whole` false means exactly nothing changed.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `whole` | `bool` |  |
| `rects` | `list<rect>` |  |
